essence: It is a victory-litany: twenty-four *jaya*-cries that praise the Lord by letting every attribute stand absolute — names (2–3), body and feet (4), beauty and adornment (5–8), duping and embrace (9), greed for gifts (10), outlasting the gods (11), sealing worlds and giving the self (12), secondlessness with a helper (13), stride and song (14), need-free height (15), unopposed terror (16), play and anger (17), lamp and wakefulness (18), cave-hum and mind-sky (19), gold-mountain and portent-moon (20), missed-by-austerity and seen-by-madness (21), leafing and fondling (22), sole doing and lotus-festival (23) — until the cries themselves run to thirteen and end in the three-eyed One (24).

rasa.justification: The sthāyibhāva is devotion (bhakti) in the mode of acclamation (jaya); the vyabhicāri is wonder (camatkāra) at the Lord's attributes. The rasa is the heroism of praise — each cry performs conquest over silence. Twenty-four jaya-cries that praise the Lord by letting every attribute stand absolute: names, body, feet, beauty, adornment, duping, embrace, greed for gifts, outlasting gods, sealing worlds, giving self, secondlessness with helper, stride, song, need-free height, unopposed terror, play, anger, lamp, wakefulness, cave-hum, mind-sky, gold-mountain, portent-moon, missed-by-austerity, seen-by-madness, leafing, fondling, sole doing, lotus-festival — until the cries run to thirteen and end in the three-eyed One. Abhinava's rasa theory frames this as vīra: the relish (camatkāra) of the Absolute celebrated, not argued. Lakshmanjoo's commentary: the victory-litany converts understanding into praise.
